title: Light Up the Parlor
objective: Children will look closely at a Victorian parlor on Christmas Eve, first cold and dark, then warm and bright, and name what is in it. They will hear that long ago Christmas was hardly celebrated, and that a story by Charles Dickens, *A Christmas Carol*, helped make it a time for kindness, sharing and being together.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Long ago, a story about kindness helped make Christmas a time to open our hearts to other people. Kindness is something every child can give.

items.text: name three things in a Victorian Christmas parlor: the tree, the fire and the clock
items.question: name three things in the parlor?
items.screen: name three things in the parlor

items.text: tell how the parlor changed from cold and dark to warm and bright
items.question: tell how the room changed?

materials: The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
A battery tea light or flashlight, to ‘light’ the room
Crayons, including yellow and orange, and the differentiated handouts
questions: What do you see in the room? Let’s name everything we can find.
Is the room warm or cold? How can you tell?
What do people do to make a room feel welcoming?
*A Christmas Carol* is a story about kindness. What kind thing could you do today?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in *Dickens’ Christmas Parlour*, children open each part of a Victorian Christmas — the clock, the tree, the cards, the book, the window and the fire — and watch the cold room come to life.
**Make a card:** in the *Christmas Card Maker*, choose a robin, a wreath or a snowy church for the front.

steps.title: A cold, dark room
script: Dim the lights. Show the cold parlor. Say: *“This is a room in a house long ago, on the night before Christmas. Look at this room. Is it warm or cold? Light or dark?”* Let children name what they see: a chair, a window with snow, a little tree, a fireplace with no fire. *“It looks lonely. What would make it feel warm?”*

screen.alt: A dark, cold parlor at night: an empty grate, a Christmas tree with unlit candles by a snowy window

steps.purpose: Wonder at a room before anything is explained.
students: Look at this room. Is it warm or cold? Light or dark?
What can you see in it?

steps.title: Warm and bright
script: Switch on the tea light and show the warm parlor beside the cold one. *“What changed?”* The fire is blazing in the grate; the candles on the Christmas tree are lit; the whole room glows. Play *I spy*: children point to the fire, the tree with its candles, the clock on the mantelpiece, the snowy window and the holly over the fireplace. Count the things you find together.

items.label: Cold and dark
items.alt: A dark, cold parlor at night: an empty grate, a Christmas tree with unlit candles by a snowy window

items.label: Warm and bright
items.alt: The same parlor glowing: a fire blazing in the grate and the candles lit on the Christmas tree

steps.purpose: See what a Victorian Christmas brought into the room by comparing the two pictures.
students: Find the fire. Find the tree. Find the clock.

steps.title: Long ago
script: Show the snowy village. Tell it simply: long ago, in Victorian Britain, Christmas was hardly celebrated. Many people worked such long hours that there was little time to celebrate. Then Queen Victoria and her husband, Prince Albert, helped make the Christmas tree popular, and people began to send Christmas cards.

screen.alt: A painting of a snowy Victorian village street at dusk: snow-covered houses with lit windows, a church spire, two tall Christmas trees, and people walking in the snow
screen.caption: The snowy village from the exhibition’s second poster

steps.purpose: Hear that Christmas was once hardly celebrated, and how trees and cards arrived.
students: Can you see the Christmas trees?

steps.title: A story about kindness
script: A writer named Charles Dickens wrote a story called *A Christmas Carol*. In it, a man called Scrooge changes, and learns to be kind. People loved the story, and it helped make Christmas a time to open our hearts to others: *a story about being kind, sharing, and being together.*

screen.text:
A story about being kind,
sharing, and being together

steps.purpose: Meet the message at the heart of the parlor: kindness, sharing and being together.
students: How does it feel when someone is kind to you?

steps.title: Your handout
script: Each child works on a handout. All three show the cold room and the warm room, and ask which is warm and bright.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Picture-led. Circle the warm room, find the fire, the tree and the clock, draw a flame on each candle, trace *KIND*.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: A little more. Circle the warm room, circle what changed, light and count the candles, copy *KIND* under a model.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Draw and tell. Tell a grown-up three things that changed, draw a kind thing to do, design a card front, finish *I can be kind by…*

steps.purpose: Find, light and share on paper, at the right level for each child.
students: Which room is warm and bright? Find it on your page.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the questions on the screen. For each one, the children show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now name three things in the parlor? Can you tell how the room changed? Can you name a kind thing you could do?”*

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.

steps.title: Share a kindness
script: Then say: *“A Christmas Carol is a story about kindness. Hold up your hands to a warm fire. Tell a partner one kind thing you could do for someone today.”*
